/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.headline: Schools’ duty to respond to sexual abuse is now law, ministers say
/education/2026/oct/04/child-on-child-se.bodyHtml:
A government spokesperson described the figures as appalling. ‘No child should be unsafe at school, and no child should have to carry this alone. That is why schools’ duty to respond to sexual violence and harassment is now statutory, and why staff are trained to spot concerns early and support victims.

‘As part of our strategy to halve violence against women and girls, we have pledged to make sure all young people are taught about healthy relationships and consent from an early age – and we’ve forced tech companies to tackle harmful content and protect young people online through the Online Safety Act.’

Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the ‘horrifying’ scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s, including multiple rapes, are reported to police every year.

Close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded on average by police every day in primary and secondary schools in England and Wales, according to Guardian analysis of police data for 2021-25.

The figures include reports of almost 2,000 rapes and attempted rapes, which is equivalent to an average of one allegation of rape at a school received by the police every single day. More than a third of the rape victims were children under 13.

The new data showed at least 8,500 sexual offences against under-13s were recorded by police as having occurred on school premises or nearby between 2021 and 2025 – equivalent to 4.7 offences reported each day.

While most of the police reports did not specify the age of the alleged perpetrator, they are likely to be fellow pupils, and in at least 1,890 of the offences reported as being committed against under-13s the offender was described as under 18.

Girls are more likely to be victims of sexual offences than boys, according to the analysis, which found that close to two-thirds of reported crimes affecting under-13s where the sex of the victim was documented had involved female victims.

Responding to the figures, the children’s commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, described peer-on-peer abuse in schools as ‘widespread, normalised and too often brushed under the carpet’.

‘We have taken important steps in the last few years,’ she said. ‘But as these figures show we have a long way to go. This is not simply a school or college issue, it is a societal one.’

The data, obtained via freedom of information requests, also includes reports of a further 6,140 crimes involving the possession, taking, making or distribution of indecent or prohibited images of children under 18.

This has become a significant problem in schools, particularly with the introduction of AI and deepfakes, but headteachers are hoping phone bans and social media restrictions will help to turn the tide.

Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors who represents survivors of sexual abuse, said: ‘This new dataset evidences clearly the horrifying true scale of sexual abuse of children within schools.

‘Those in authority can no longer claim that they were not aware of how prevalent an issue this is. Parents deserve to know that their children are safe while undertaking their education, and anything short of concrete action to tackle this problem is simply not good enough.’

The data also detailed reports of at least 2,300 sexual crimes against children aged 13 to 16 and a further 9,100 sexual crimes against those aged 13 or over recorded by police as having happened in or in the vicinity of schools between 2021 and 2025. Three-quarters of these involved a female victim.

The true figure is likely to be significantly higher, since the analysis is based on data provided by 33 police forces that replied to FoI requests, out of a total of 43 in England and Wales. There may also be variation in the ways forces collect data.

Janaya Walker, interim director of the End Violence Against Women (EVAW) campaign, said: ‘This data is shocking but sadly not surprising, and underlines the urgent need to protect children from sexual violence at school.

‘We’ve long raised the alarm about this national crisis in schools. However, despite what should have been numerous watershed moments, young people continue to be harmed en masse.’

Excluding 2021, when schools were closed between January and March due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the rate of sexual offences increased by four per cent outside London, with 26.6 offences per 100,000 children under 13 in 2022, rising to 27.6 in 2025.

Acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said the number of sexual offences reported in school settings was ‘deeply concerning’, but might also reflect growing awareness and greater confidence among child victims to come forward and report what has happened to them.

‘These findings underline the urgent need for a stronger focus on prevention through age-appropriate education, digital resilience, effective safeguarding measures and greater support for parents, schools and professionals to identify concerns early and intervene before harm occurs,’ she said.

‘Tackling child sexual abuse requires a whole-system response, with policing, education, social care, health services, technology companies and communities working together to prevent harm, protect children and hold offenders to account.’

Soma Sara is the chief executive and founder of the Everyone’s Invited campaign, which has played a key role in highlighting sexual violence in schools. She now runs education programmes for young people. ‘When we first launched [in 2020], people refused to even refer to rape culture,’ she said.

‘It is now accepted as an issue both in wider society and within our schools. But we cannot expect schools to tackle it alone, particularly when the online world is changing so rapidly.

‘The proliferation of violent pornography and the increasing harms young people are exposed to online are creating challenges that are incredibly difficult for teachers to keep pace with.’

Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: ‘The prevalence of these incidents is simply appalling and a source of great concern for everyone working in education.

‘We hope measures being taken by the government to better protect children online will improve matters but ministers must be prepared to go further in regulating online platforms.’

Figures from some forces were taken from keyword searches of police summary notes, so may include cases that mentioned schools but happened outside school premises. Some other forces recorded schools as a location for crimes both on and nearby school premises.

/us-news/2026/oct/04/us-bombers-sent-hom.headline: Investigation leads police to six arrests over suspected Fairford plot
/us-news/2026/oct/04/us-bombers-sent-hom.bodyHtml:
The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.

Police investigating a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September arrested a dual British-Iranian national in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation.

The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.

A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.”

At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat.

There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire.

According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base.

A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces.

“One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.”

British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement.

RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160km) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

Its use in recent months came after then prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran.

The US military still maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October.

/politics/2026/oct/04/green-party-votes-.headline: Equalities challenge to Green party’s Zionism vote has ‘good chance’, KC says
/politics/2026/oct/04/green-party-votes-.bodyHtml:
The Greens have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state, a move opposed by the bulk of the party’s MPs and which is expected to face legal challenge.

It is understood that some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation.

Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success.

‘I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,’ he said.

Zionism when defined in the broad sense of supporting a Jewish nation state ‘is likely to be a protected belief’ under the act, he said.

Four of the party’s five MPs opposed the motion. Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns said they were ‘deeply saddened’ while Siân Berry and Carla Denyer said they would support any Jewish members who believed they were being targeted as a result of the policy change.

After the vote, the party’s five MPs, plus Polanski and his two co-deputy leaders, released a joint statement saying the party ‘will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment’, adding: ‘We know there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.’

However, Ramsay, Chowns, Berry and Denyer all posted this on social media with messages noting their opposition to the motion.

The binding policy motion, passed by 1,022 votes to 813, says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be ‘treated as any other form of racism’. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state ‘with equal rights for all’.

Israel’s foreign ministry said the resolution ‘constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination’.

Foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to declare Green party leader Zack Polanski barred from entering Israel, the ministry said, adding the decision had been coordinated with the relevant authorities.

While opinion among Jewish Green members is split, some have expressed worry that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues.

After the vote, one backer of the motion, Salma Yaqoob, a former member of George Galloway’s Respect party who is now a Green, insisted this would not happen, saying: ‘Nobody will be removed, challenged, disciplined, suspended because they put forward or articulate their belief in Zionism.’

However, an amendment put forward saying the motion should not be used to ‘pressure, proscribe or discipline members based on affiliation with Jewish community institutions’ was voted down.

The motion argues that Zionism is necessarily racist as it ‘privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others’. It adds: ‘This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism, as defined, and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists. Not all Jews are Zionists and not all Zionists are Jews …

‘Zionism, as defined above, will be treated as any other form of racism, and this motion will be implemented by the anti-racism policy working group as appropriate and in accordance with its ordinary practice.’

According to the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, about two-thirds of British Jews consider themselves Zionists.

Zack Polanski, who heads the Greens in England and Wales and missed the vote at the party’s conference in Brighton to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has faced criticism for a perceived lack of leadership on a hugely divisive issue.

There have also been concerns that the policy change was pushed largely by newcomers who have little interest in the rest of the party’s platform.

During the lengthy debate, which was for members only, Chowns and Caroline Lucas, the former leader who was the Greens’ first MP, argued against the plan.

The motion had been pushed by a group called Greens for Palestine, which encouraged non-party members to sign up to the party to make sure the policy was debated and adopted. After it was passed, supporters came to the front of the hall to hug and cheer.

One member who opposed the motion said: ‘There are now two Green parties – the everyday members, and those who have joined for just one reason, Palestine, and who have no interest in anything else.’

There is considerable disquiet among some senior Greens who feel that Polanski, who is Jewish, could have taken a stronger stance on the issue. The party leader has justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza during Israel’s assault on the territory.

Asked on Saturday if he believed Zionism was racist, Polanski told the BBC: ‘Well, in the motion, it is defined as the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people. I think that is clearly racism.’

The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the main Jewish denominations in the UK, condemned the vote, saying: ‘The motion is antisemitic in its formulation and intention. By adopting it, the Green party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party.

‘Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews. The Green party has chosen to brand Jews who hold this belief as racists and make their equal participation in the party conditional on renouncing it.’

Adam Langleben, who coordinated complaints from the Jewish Labour Movement to the Equality and Human Rights Commission, said: ‘This is without doubt the most antisemitic and racist motion brought before a mainstream political party in my lifetime. It is Corbynism on steroids, and would seem even more open to legal challenge.’

/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.headline: Refugee Council welcomes new safe routes, calls for wider access
/uk-news/2026/oct/04/women-small-boats-r.bodyHtml:
Imran Hussain, a director at the Refugee Council, welcomed the home secretary’s acknowledgment of widespread sexual violence, but questioned why the government had closed safe and legal routes which could help asylum seekers avoid falling into the hands of predators.

‘We know from our services that women and girls fleeing war and persecution face sexual violence both in the conflicts they have escaped and on the journeys they are forced to make in search of safety,’ he said.

‘That is why in welcoming the government’s announcement last week of new safe routes we called for them not to be limited to a few hundred people. Last year the government closed family reunion, the safe route for refugees which overwhelmingly benefits women and children.

‘It is entirely right to talk about the dangers women face on these journeys but we should not be closing the safe routes that could keep them out of harm’s way. Protecting women means more safe routes, not fewer.’

Nearly all women who try to reach the UK in small boats from northern France have been raped on their journey, Shabana Mahmood has claimed.

In an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast, the home secretary said far-right, balaclava-wearing activists would ‘kill’ or ‘kick me out of my own country’ if they took power.

Speaking to the former Tory minister Rory Stewart and Tony Blair’s former close adviser Alastair Campbell, she said sexual abusers would exploit most asylum seekers as long as traffickers continued to decide who came to the UK.

She said: ‘We’re not in control of this border. The sifting of the people that end up in the north of France and are about to get on a dinghy is done by criminal gangs who are also, by the way, people traffickers.

‘You can almost guarantee that every woman that’s in the north of France has probably been raped along the journey. Some of the men too, they’ve certainly been abused and threatened. That is not the model that should decide whether somebody gets to come to the UK, make this their place of sanctuary and ultimately become one of us.’

Asked by Campbell about balaclava-wearing protesters shutting down ports and praising her policies, she said they should ‘sod off’.

She added: ‘They’re just troublemakers. You know, they’d kill me in a minute if they could, and they’d definitely kick me out of my own country. So let’s just be really clear about who and what they are. They don’t think I’m a true Brit and they hate the fact that I’m a Muslim.’

Mahmood also said she considered herself ‘part of the pro-Palestinian cause’ and felt ‘very uncomfortable’ over the arrests of activists opposing the ban imposed on Palestine Action.

Merseyside police arrested 82 people on Monday at the Labour party conference on suspicion of wearing or carrying articles supporting a proscribed organisation.

In a protest organised by Defend Our Juries, scores of people sat outside the conference centre in Liverpool, many holding handmade banners saying they supported Palestine Action.

Mahmood said: ‘For those of us who have been in the pro-Palestinian cause all of our lives, these are people – sometimes you’ll know who they are, you know, you’ve been on the marches with them – it feels very uncomfortable to see them falling foul of section 13 of the Terrorism Act.’

However, she defended enforcing the ban, regardless of her views: ‘You’ve got to be able to apply your principles, even when it’s uncomfortable for you, because you’re going to really want to apply them when it’s something you, you know, with your whole heart, are feeling very passionately about.’

Authorities were preparing on Sunday for the arrival of a migrant dinghy heading for the south coast. The boat was being shadowed by French coastguard and rescue vessels and moving toward the Channel boundary line, according to ship tracking data.

It appeared to have set off from near the Utah Beach area of Normandy on Sunday morning.

Caroline Dinenage, the Conservative MP for Gosport in Hampshire, said there was ‘nothing to suggest’ the boat would land on the county’s coast but police were ‘making preparations should that situation change’.

A government spokesperson said: ‘The Border Security Command works around the clock to monitor the Channel and protect our border. It is vital we continue to detain, check and process every small boat arrival.’

/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.headline: Lula vows fresh campaign push as Brazil heads into runoff vote
/world/2026/oct/05/brazil-presidential-r.bodyHtml:
Lula has vowed to fight on in a fresh campaign, after Brazil’s presidential race went to a second round, with the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beating the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but falling short of the outright majority needed to avoid a runoff.

Speaking in Sāo Paulo, Lula put a brave face on a difficult night for the left. “We have just had a lesson in Brazilian democracy,” he said. “The result is often unexpected. We can never get everything we wanted. I confess to you that I was convinced I was going to win the election in the first round … But we have a second round.”

Lula said Bolsonaro’s “dark past” would become clearer to voters in the lead-up to that vote. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil.”

With 99.9 per cent of votes counted, the 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president, Jair Bolsonaro, had won 47 per cent, meaning he will now face a 25 October showdown with his 80-year-old rival. Lula received 45.1 per cent. Bolsonaro received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m.

Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite and is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, who included Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1 per cent, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2 per cent.

Brazil’s far-right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan, was elected to the lower house of congress. Bolsonaro’s former infrastructure minister, Tarcísio de Freitas, was reelected as governor of São Paulo, Brazil’s most populous and economically important state.

Of the 54 senators elected, 34 were from the right or far right.

Flávio Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital, Brasília, that the result signalled “the end of an era” for Lula’s Workers’ party. “Lula has fought seven presidential elections. He’s worried about power. I am worried about the future of Brazil,” he said.

Earlier, as he cast this vote, Lula said Latin America’s largest democracy faced a stark choice, highlighting his adversary’s well-documented links to members of Rio’s underworld, including once employing close relatives of a notorious contract killer.

Lula, who became Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002 and was returned to office in 2006 and 2022, is hoping to secure a historic fourth non-consecutive term in this year’s election.

Allies of the veteran leftwinger called the election a crucial battle in the fight against a far-right movement that less than four years ago brought chaos to the capital, Brasília, during an unsuccessful attempt to overturn the result of the 2022 election, when Lula beat the incumbent president, Jair Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro hopes winning the presidency will allow him to free his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after refusing to accept he had lost the last election to Lula. Ahead of the election he also called for tactical voting from conservatives who are not supporters of Bolsonarismo, but want to vote Lula out of power.

As well as the president, Brazil’s nearly 159 million voters were choosing state parliamentarians, 27 state governors, 513 members of the lower house and 54 members of the 81-seat senate. Bolsonaro supporters made the senate race a priority because senators are the only lawmakers who can impeach supreme court justices – a demand among Bolsonaristas since the court jailed the former president for attempting a coup.

Hundreds of leftwingers had gathered at the heart of Laranjeiras, one of Rio’s most leftwing neighbourhoods, hoping to celebrate a Lula win to the sound of samba. But the mood soured and tears were shed as the hours passed and Bolsonaro’s lead over Lula held.

“It’s so sad that the Brazilian people … have opted for so much retrogression,” said Marcelo Mac, one of the owners of Miolo, a leftwing bar in Laranjeiras, as the scale of the rightwing advance was confirmed on Sunday night.

Mac, 46, voiced perplexity that the son of the man who tried to stage a coup only four years ago was now in pole position to become Brazil’s next leader. “He’s such an abominable guy that he manages to be even worse than his father,” Mac said of Bolsonaro.

Beside the bar a yellow flag stamped with Lula’s face carried the slogan: “Turn left”. But Brazil had voted for a turn to the far right.

Bolsonaro seemed to have the wind in his sails in the final days before Sunday’s vote, amid public frustration at a cost of living crisis and urban violence.

But opinion polls failed to predict the scale of the rightwing triumph.

Shop assistant Italo Andrade dos Santos, a 31-year-old Bolsonaro voter, had to keep his celebrations restrained behind the counter of the pharmacy where he was working a Sunday night shift. “I was a little disappointed because I expected Flávio to win in the first round. But I’m happy he’s ahead,” said Santos, adding that he voted “more to get Lula out than for Flávio himself”.

Donald Trump became a key election issue, with Lula accusing the US president of trying to swing the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour in order to “colonise” Brazil and appropriate its natural resources. Bolsonaro has vowed to build a closer relationship with Trump, who hopes a rightwing victory will help him further cement US control over Latin America after the election of pro-Trump leaders in a succession of countries, including Chile, Colombia and Peru.

/business/2026/oct/05/british-government.headline: Experts set out five-point plan to strengthen UK’s food security
/business/2026/oct/05/british-government.bodyHtml:
Academics, business leaders, community groups and food partnerships are urging the new government to treat food as a national security issue and work to make the UK’s food system more resilient, in a era when food supplies ‘can be weaponised’, they caution.

The letter calls on ministers to do the following.

  • Establish a new system of local food resilience committees under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004.

  • Audit the UK’s reliance on a few very large food companies and food imports.

  • Realign national food production around nutritional needs.

  • Create national, regional, local and community food storage schemes.

  • Support the decentralisation of the UK’s food supply.

Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages, according to a warning from more than 150 experts delivered to Andy Burnham.

The climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, cyber-attacks and energy outages are among the threats to food chain security, according to the open letter, which claims the government is ‘complacent about food as a national security matter’.

The signatories warn that the ‘just-in-time’ delivery system built up over recent decades ‘is not fit for today’s or tomorrow’s challenges’, as little stock is held along the food supply chain and the UK does not have any national food storage. Ministers wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s.

‘The food system is exposed to shocks and threats from geopolitics, climate heating, ransomware, energy outages, software malfunction and disinformation,’ according to the letter.

The experts go on to warn: ‘These shocks will fall upon a system that is highly wasteful, import-dependent, environmentally unsustainable, and driven by the pursuit of private profit rather than resilience, with millions of people unable to afford a decent, healthy diet.’

The warning comes weeks after the National Audit Office, the public spending watchdog, issued a rebuke to ministers, accusing them of failing to do enough to help households and businesses plan for possible emergencies.

The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, while the UK is more reliant on food imports than some of its neighbours.

The letter claims the government is not paying enough attention to what such a store should look like, and is failing to consider that many lower-income households may not be able to afford to build up a stockpile.

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, recently recommended that UK households build up stores of enough food and water to survive a few days without power or water, amid warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a wet, stormy winter to the UK.

One of the signatories, Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, said: ‘We need a system shift: grow more food; more regionalism, diversity and storage at multiple levels, not just households; and public engagement in civil food defence. Central government must provide more strategic leadership while encouraging actions at different levels. Communities and households cannot resolve faultlines in the UK’s food system.’

Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who also signed the letter, said: ‘Food resilience, healthy diet and environmental benefits all point in the same direction: grow more of the vegetables, fruit and pulses people actually need, closer to home.’

The Cabinet Office is to launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for future emergencies.

The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include assembling items at home that could include tinned meat, fruit or vegetables that do not need cooking.

Eagle has said she would oversee farming improvements and a reservoir-building programme that should help Britain face extreme weather.

/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.headline: Apache says contingency plans will limit impact of North Sea strike
/business/2026/oct/05/strikes-by-north-s.bodyHtml:
Apache also said it had contingency plans in place, and that it did not expect any strike action to affect other producers and their ability to operate through the Forties pipeline system. The plans included keeping ‘experienced personnel’ on key sites, and it said any reduction in pipeline pressure as a result of industrial action would be similar to what occurred during routine maintenance outages.

‘As a responsible operator, we are planning to maintain safe operations throughout any industrial action,’ Apache added.

A looming strike by oil workers in the North Sea could ‘severely disrupt’ UK fuel supplies, the Unite union has said, adding that staff were left with no choice after a breakdown in pay talks with the Texas oil company Apache.

That could ultimately result in the entire Forties pipeline system in the North Sea – which is said to handle almost a third of the UK’s oil and gas – ‘going down’, the union said, adding that the disruption could also ripple out and affect other large North Sea operators.

Any action would affect the Forties and Beryl oilfields, and could lead to one of the critical North Sea platforms, known as Charlie, ‘being brought to a standstill’, Unite said.

Apache said it had ‘engaged constructively throughout the pay discussions’ and added that it had offered a four per cent pay increase for staff, ‘whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year’.

‘We believe our final offer to the union is fair and recognises the contribution of our offshore workforce, alongside the wider benefits in our total rewards package,’ Apache said. ‘The proposed pay increase is also in line with that awarded to our non-unionised employees earlier this year.’

The union said Apache workers had ‘emphatically’ backed strike action after being given what it said was an unacceptable pay offer that amounted to a real-terms pay cut for many employees, at a time when the company was ‘raking in eye-watering profits’.

Unite said the operator had also set deadlines for reaching an agreement over back pay and indicated payments could be withheld, ‘leaving workers potentially thousands of pounds out of pocket’.

Unite blamed the potential disruption on Apache’s failure to reach a pay deal, saying the company’s behaviour could have ‘far-reaching consequences for workers, operators and consumers’.

Commenting on the potential strike action, the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham, said: ‘We will not tolerate unacceptable pay offers.’

Stevie Davies, a Unite industrial officer, said any disruption to Apache’s platforms ‘would have a direct hit on the Forties pipeline and potentially severely affect the UK’s fuel supplies’.

Strike action could begin later this month, according to the union, and could involve more than 160 Apache offshore workers, including electrical experts, production technicians and radio operators.

The Texas-based APA Corporation, which is the parent company behind Apache North Sea Production, reported $1.4bn (£1.1bn) in after-tax profits and $9.2bn in revenues for last year.

Consumers have already been grappling with rising fuel and gas prices because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has been disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf.

On Friday, British motorists were dealt a fresh blow when it emerged that the average price of diesel had climbed to a record £2 a litre.

At the same time it was announced that leaders of G7 nations would release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.

Planned strikes by Neo Next offshore workers, organised by Unite, were called off this summer after they secured a deal that the union said lifted the pay package by more than £4,000. The deal was reached days before workers were due to start a series of strikes from 22 July.

Ineos, which operates the Forties pipeline system, was contacted for comment.

/money/2026/oct/05/scammers-hijacking-uk.headline: Report Fraud urges switch to passkeys to protect social media accounts
/money/2026/oct/05/scammers-hijacking-uk.bodyHtml:
Report Fraud is launching an awareness campaign urging the public to protect their online accounts from hackers by switching to passkeys where they are available. A passkey uses an individual’s device and biometrics to authenticate them and cannot be hacked like a password.

The total amount stolen by criminals who hack into people’s emails and social media accounts and then pretend to be them has risen by more than 400 per cent in a year, official UK data shows.

In many cases, the scammers are hijacking people’s accounts in order to use their identity to sell fake event tickets – such as to sold-out gigs – to unsuspecting friends and family.

The total reported amount stolen via email and social media account hacking reached £6.3m in the 2025-26 financial year, compared with £1.2m in 2024-25, according to the Report Fraud service run by the City of London police, which holds national responsibility for economic crime.

However, the true total may be much higher as many scam victims do not report the crime, often because they feel embarrassed, and sometimes because the individual amount of money involved was relatively small.

The Guardian previously featured the case of a music fan whose Instagram account was targeted by hackers, who used her identity to advertise tickets to an Oasis gig and stole £1,400 from her friends. She said the hackers impersonated her so well that her friends and family genuinely thought they were speaking to her.

Others have been scammed by fraudulent WhatsApp and text messages in which a criminal pretends to be their child or a relative who is in an emergency situation and urgently needs cash. This has been dubbed the ‘Hi mum’ scam.

Data from Santander has shown that among customers of the bank, fraudsters pretending to be someone’s son were the most successful at extracting cash, followed by daughters.

Ch Supt Amanda Wolf, head of Report Fraud operations, said: ‘For most people, being hacked isn’t just a cyber issue – it’s personal. It can leave victims locked out of important accounts, worried about what information has been accessed, and concerned that criminals may use their identity to target others.’

She added that what starts with one compromised account ‘can quickly impact family, friends and colleagues as fraudsters exploit trusted relationships to commit further fraud’.

/politics/2026/oct/04/tories-scrap-envir.headline: Tories pledge £50,000 cheaper homes under deregulation drive
/politics/2026/oct/04/tories-scrap-envir.bodyHtml:
In a slew of announcements at the Conservative party conference on Monday, the Tories will pledge measures that they claim would cut the price of a new home by £50,000, including scrapping net zero regulations on housebuilding such as the Future Homes Standard, which requires all new homes in England to be zero-carbon ready.

The Conservatives will announce a bonfire of regulations, including abolishing affordable homes and community funding rules as well as scrapping Natural England and the Environment Agency.

The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, will say the party intends to ‘streamline regulations’ that protect nature and oblige developers to include affordable homes and community services such as GP surgeries, in order to speed up infrastructure and housebuilding.

The announcements on Monday are a signal that the party intends to refocus on the economy, an area where it has made relatively little progress in the polls.

Tory strategists believe there is a major opening to make gains against Reform and Labour, given the limited focus on growth from Andy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, at the Labour conference last week.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, published a new tract on Sunday called The Right Way, which she said would be the bedrock that underpinned the party’s policy development before the next election. Polls have the party still trailing third behind Labour and Reform UK.

Introducing the document – inspired by Margaret Thatcher’s The Right Approach from 1976 – Badenoch said the Conservatives still expected to win the next election and needed to ‘hit the ground running … We will need to be ready from day one, having already shown people what kind of government we are going to be.’

‘Keir Starmer didn’t have a plan. That’s why he’s gone,’ she said. ‘Andy Burnham doesn’t have one either and that is why I know the announcements he is making will all come to naught. We have to be different, different from Labour, and different from the party we were two years ago.’

The party will promise to replace section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy that oblige developers to build a proportion of affordable housing and support school and health service demands locally. Instead, Griffith will say, there will be a ‘one stop’ levy on developers.

The party has also pledged to abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency, ‘moving to a more streamlined regulatory landscape to protect our environment’.

Griffith will say in his first speech as shadow chancellor that the Tories would continue to back the expansion of Heathrow airport and leave the Aarhus convention, which makes it easier for community groups to oppose developments.

Conservative shadow Treasury ministers will be tasked with finding new ways of simplifying tax for individuals and businesses, Griffith will say, calling the tax code ‘a cat’s cradle of complexity’.

In his speech, he will say: ‘No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation.

‘Our task just got bigger. We face a prime minister that wants to return Britain to an imagined past. A socialist fever dream of the 1970s. Cheaper homes, lower taxes and less red tape. This will be the most ambitious deregulation project in a generation. We will be more prepared than ever before. We will set out our plans line by line. Every bill, every regulation, every chapter.’

Griffith will say that the government must speed up the building of a Heathrow third runway in whatever way it can. ‘I refuse to accept for a single moment that the country of Brunel and Bazalgette, of the vaccine taskforce and the Mulberry harbours, has to sit around waiting until the 2040s to get a third runway built,’ he will say.

Burnham has recently expressed personal scepticism about the Heathrow third runway, saying he would take differing views seriously.

The new shadow housing secretary, Katie Lam, will say the scrapping of housing regulations and of enforcement bodies would mean ‘anti-growth ideologues can never again hold our country hostage’.

The party said Natural England and the Environment Agency were preventing too many homes being built and adding unnecessary costs to building. Both bodies would be scrapped, with their necessary functions brought directly into Defra.
